gaps.name: Ticker timer
gaps.what: A ticker timer marks tape at a fixed rate (often 50 dots per second, so 0.02 s apart). Dot spacing gives speed; changing spacing shows acceleration.
gaps.check: A tape has dots 4.0 cm apart from a 50 Hz ticker timer. What is the speed?
gaps.answer: Time between dots is 0.02 s, so speed = 0.040 / 0.02 = 2.0 m/s.

gaps.name: Air-track gliders
gaps.what: Gliders float on a cushion of air so friction is almost removed; used to test momentum conservation and Newton's second law with light gates.
gaps.check: Why is an air-track used rather than a bench for a collision experiment?
gaps.answer: It makes friction negligible, so there is no external horizontal force and momentum is conserved.

gaps.name: Collision practical with trolleys
gaps.what: Measure velocities of trolleys before and after a collision (light gates, card length over time, or video), then compare total momentum before and after.
gaps.check: Describe how to test conservation of momentum with two trolleys.
gaps.answer: Measure masses; time cards through light gates before and after impact to get velocities; compare sum of mv before and after.

gaps.name: g by electromagnet and trapdoor
gaps.what: Electromagnet release starts the timer; ball hitting the trapdoor stops it. Vary height h, plot h against t squared: gradient = g/2. Residual magnetism delays release (systematic error).
gaps.check: In the trapdoor method, what is the gradient of a graph of h against t squared?
gaps.answer: g/2 (from s = ½gt² with u = 0), so g = 2 × gradient.

gaps.name: Speed from a light gate
gaps.what: A light gate times how long a card (or object) of known length blocks the beam; speed = card length ÷ blocked time. Two gates or a double card give acceleration.
gaps.check: A 5.0 cm card blocks a light gate for 0.025 s. What is its speed?

gaps.name: Terminal velocity practical details
gaps.what: Ball-bearing in viscous liquid (rubber bands as markers) or paper cones in air. Terminal velocity reached when equal distances take equal times; place first marker well below the surface.
gaps.check: How can you show a ball-bearing falling in oil has reached terminal velocity?
gaps.answer: Time it over successive equal distances between markers; equal times mean constant (terminal) velocity.

gaps.name: Finding centre of gravity experimentally
gaps.what: Hang a flat (lamina) object from a point with a plumb line, mark the vertical; repeat from another point. The centre of gravity is where the lines cross.
gaps.check: How do you find the centre of gravity of an irregular card?
gaps.answer: Suspend it from two different points; draw the plumb-line vertical each time; the intersection is the centre of gravity.

gaps.name: Rubber bands and polythene strips
gaps.what: Rubber does not obey Hooke's law and its unloading curve lies below loading (energy dissipated as heat). Polythene strips deform plastically and thin (neck) before breaking.
gaps.check: Why does a stretched rubber band warm up after repeated loading and unloading?
gaps.answer: The unloading curve lies below the loading curve; the area between them is energy transferred to thermal energy.

gaps.name: Young modulus method details
gaps.what: Use a long thin wire so extension is measurable; measure diameter with a micrometer at several points; read extension with a marker against a fixed scale; wear goggles in case the wire snaps.
gaps.check: Why is the wire in a Young modulus experiment long and thin?
gaps.answer: Long gives larger extension for the same strain; thin gives larger stress for a given load, so extension is easier to measure.

gaps.name: Ripple tank demonstrations
gaps.what: A ripple tank with a lamp above shows wavefronts on a screen; a stroboscope freezes them. Shows reflection off barriers, refraction over shallow regions, diffraction through gaps, interference from two dippers.
gaps.check: How is refraction shown in a ripple tank?
gaps.answer: Place a glass plate to make a shallow region; waves slow there, wavelength shortens and wavefronts change direction.

gaps.name: Microwave kit
gaps.what: Microwave transmitters emit plane-polarised waves (wavelength about 3 cm); a metal grille blocks them when its rods are parallel to the electric field; the receiver measures intensity.
gaps.check: A grille is rotated 90 degrees between transmitter and receiver. What happens to the signal?
gaps.answer: It changes between maximum and minimum (near zero) as the rods change from perpendicular to parallel to the oscillations.

gaps.name: Polarising filters for light
gaps.what: Light passing through one Polaroid becomes plane polarised; a second filter rotated through 90 degrees (crossed) blocks it. Reflected light is partially polarised.
gaps.check: Two polarising filters are crossed. What intensity passes, and what if one is rotated a further 90 degrees?
gaps.answer: Crossed: almost none. Rotated another 90 degrees (parallel again): maximum transmission.

gaps.name: Two-loudspeaker interference
gaps.what: Two loudspeakers driven by one signal generator are coherent; walking parallel to them you hear loud and quiet regions (constructive and destructive interference).
gaps.check: Why must both loudspeakers be connected to the same signal generator?
gaps.answer: So they have the same frequency and a constant phase difference, i.e. they are coherent.

gaps.name: Resonance tube for speed of sound
gaps.what: A tube in water is raised until the note from a tuning fork resonates loudly; first resonance length is about a quarter wavelength (plus end correction). The difference between successive resonances is λ/2.
gaps.check: First and second resonance lengths are 0.18 m and 0.54 m at 480 Hz. Find v.
gaps.answer: Difference 0.36 m = λ/2, so λ = 0.72 m and v = 480 × 0.72 ≈ 350 m/s.

gaps.name: Stationary waves on a string apparatus
gaps.what: A vibration generator (driven by a signal generator) vibrates a string passing over a pulley with hanging masses; adjusting frequency gives stationary-wave patterns with nodes at the fixed ends.
gaps.check: On a 1.2 m string fixed at both ends, three loops form at 60 Hz. What is the wave speed?
gaps.answer: Three loops = 3λ/2 = 1.2 m so λ = 0.80 m; v = 60 × 0.80 = 48 m/s.

gaps.name: Microwaves and a reflector
gaps.what: Microwaves reflected from a metal plate superpose with the incident waves to form a stationary wave; moving a probe receiver finds nodes λ/2 apart.
gaps.check: A probe moves 7.5 cm between the 1st and 6th nodes. What is the wavelength?
gaps.answer: That is 5 node spacings: 5 × λ/2 = 7.5 cm, so λ = 3.0 cm.

gaps.name: Ray box and semicircular block
gaps.what: A ray aimed at the centre of a semicircular block's flat face travels along a radius, so it crosses the curved face undeviated; only the flat face refracts. Increase the angle to find C.
gaps.check: Why is a semicircular block useful for finding the critical angle?
gaps.answer: A ray along a radius hits the curved surface at 90°, so it isn't bent there; only the flat face matters.

gaps.name: Planck constant from LEDs: method
gaps.what: Raise p.d. until each LED just starts to glow (view through a tube to cut stray light); plot threshold V against 1/λ, gradient hc/e. No semiconductor theory needed.
gaps.check: A graph of LED threshold p.d. V against 1/λ has gradient G. Write h in terms of G.
gaps.answer: eV = hc/λ, so V = (hc/e)(1/λ); h = Ge/c.

gaps.name: Gold-leaf electroscope and zinc plate
gaps.what: Negatively charged zinc on an electroscope: UV makes the leaf fall as photoelectrons leave; bright visible light does nothing; a positively charged plate does not discharge; glass between them stops UV.
gaps.check: A negatively charged electroscope with a zinc plate is lit by intense red light. What happens and why?
gaps.answer: Nothing: red photons each have less energy than the work function, regardless of intensity.

gaps.name: Why graphite diffracts electrons
gaps.what: Diffraction is significant only when λ is similar to the gap; electron de Broglie wavelengths (around 10^-10 m) match the spacing between carbon atoms, so graphite acts as a grating.
gaps.check: Why are electrons accelerated through a few kV used rather than slow electrons?
gaps.answer: Their de Broglie wavelength becomes about the atomic spacing (~10^-10 m), so diffraction is observable.

gaps.name: Diffraction grating (AS limits)
gaps.what: A grating can also be used to measure light wavelength (sharper, brighter maxima), but the d sin θ = nλ equation is only examined at A level.
gaps.check: At AS, which equation do you use for fringes from two slits?
gaps.answer: λ = ax/D (valid when a is much smaller than D); grating equations are A level only.

gaps.name: Data-loggers and ICT
gaps.what: Data-loggers record many readings quickly at short intervals, avoid human reaction time, and feed spreadsheets for graphs and calculations (for example impulse from an F–t graph).
gaps.check: Give two advantages of a data-logger with a motion sensor over a stopwatch.
gaps.answer: Much higher sampling rate; no reaction-time error; data stored and graphed automatically.

gaps.name: Table headings and axis labels
gaps.what: Column headings and axis labels are written as quantity / unit (e.g. t / s, v / m s^-1); raw data in a column use the same number of decimal places.
gaps.check: Write a correct table heading for length measured in millimetres.
gaps.answer: length / mm (or L / mm), with values only (no units) in the column.

gaps.name: Choosing graph scales
gaps.what: Scales should spread points over more than half the grid in each direction and use easy steps (1, 2, 5); the origin need not be included unless needed.
gaps.check: Why is a scale going up in 3s a poor choice?
gaps.answer: It makes plotting and reading values awkward and error-prone; use 1, 2 or 5 steps.

gaps.name: Testing for direct proportionality
gaps.what: Direct proportion needs a straight line through the origin (or a constant ratio y/x in data). A straight line with an intercept is linear but not proportional.
gaps.check: A line on a graph is straight but has a y-intercept of 2. Is y proportional to x?
gaps.answer: No: proportionality requires the line to pass through the origin.

gaps.name: Sums and differences: add absolute uncertainties
gaps.what: When adding or subtracting measurements (e.g. a length from two scale readings), add the absolute uncertainties, not the percentages.
gaps.check: Length = 45.0 cm − 12.0 cm, each ±0.1 cm. What is the uncertainty?
gaps.answer: Add absolute values: ±0.2 cm, so length = 33.0 ± 0.2 cm.

gaps.name: Interpolation and extrapolation
gaps.what: Reading between data points (interpolation) is reliable; extending a line beyond measured data (extrapolation) assumes the trend continues and is less reliable.
gaps.check: Why might extrapolating a resistance–temperature graph to 200 °C be unreliable?
gaps.answer: The relationship may not continue beyond the measured range.

gaps.name: Repeatability and reproducibility
gaps.what: Repeatable: same person, method and kit give similar results. Reproducible: different people or methods get similar results. Both give confidence before acceptance.
gaps.check: What is the difference between repeatable and reproducible results?
gaps.answer: Repeatable: same experimenter and method agree. Reproducible: other experimenters or methods agree.

gaps.name: Correlation and valid conclusions
gaps.what: A conclusion must be supported by the data and only within the measured range; a correlation alone does not prove one variable causes the other.
gaps.check: Data show resistance rises with temperature for a wire. What may you validly conclude?
gaps.answer: Over the measured range, resistance increases with temperature; state the trend shown, not beyond.

gaps.name: Checking homogeneity of equations
gaps.what: An equation is homogeneous if both sides reduce to the same SI base units; this checks it could be correct (but numbers like ½ can't be checked).
gaps.check: Show that v² = u² + 2as is homogeneous.
gaps.answer: Each term has units m² s^-2: (m/s)², and m s^-2 × m.

gaps.name: Units of less obvious quantities
gaps.what: Resistivity Ω m; force constant N m^-1; Young modulus and stress Pa; strain no unit; intensity W m^-2; Planck constant J s; number density m^-3; refractive index no unit.
gaps.check: Give the units of resistivity, strain and the Planck constant.
gaps.answer: Ω m; no unit (a ratio); J s.

gaps.name: N s equals kg m s^-1
gaps.what: Impulse in N s and momentum in kg m s^-1 are the same unit, since 1 N = 1 kg m s^-2.
gaps.check: Show that N s is equivalent to kg m s^-1.
gaps.answer: N = kg m s^-2, so N s = kg m s^-2 × s = kg m s^-1.

gaps.name: Derived units into base units
gaps.what: Express J, W, Pa, C, V and Ω in base units by working through defining equations, e.g. V = W/A = kg m² s^-3 A^-1.
gaps.check: Express the volt in SI base units.
gaps.answer: V = J/C = (kg m² s^-2)/(A s) = kg m² s^-3 A^-1.

gaps.name: Data sheet contents
gaps.what: The booklet gives g, e, c, h, particle masses, the eV conversion, area and volume formulae, sine and cosine rules; it omits W = mg, F = ma, Ek, Ep and R = V/I.
gaps.check: Which of these must you recall: P = Fv, Ek = ½mv², R = ρL/A?
gaps.answer: Ek = ½mv² (the other two are on the data sheet).

gaps.name: Sine and cosine rules for vectors
gaps.what: For non-right-angled vector triangles use the cosine rule for the resultant's size and the sine rule for an angle (both given on the data sheet), or a scale drawing.
gaps.check: Forces of 5 N and 8 N act with 60 degrees between them. Find the resultant.
gaps.answer: Triangle angle is 120°: R² = 25 + 64 − 80cos120° = 129, R ≈ 11.4 N.

gaps.name: Scale drawing of vectors
gaps.what: Draw vectors head to tail to a stated scale with a protractor; the closing side gives the resultant, measured in length and angle. Use a large scale.
gaps.check: Why should you use a large scale in a vector scale drawing?
gaps.answer: It reduces the percentage uncertainty in measured lengths and angles.

gaps.name: Vector subtraction and change in velocity
gaps.what: To subtract a vector, add its reverse. Change in velocity = final − initial, so a reversal of direction gives a change larger than either speed.
gaps.check: A ball hits a wall at 6 m/s and rebounds at 4 m/s. What is the change in velocity?
gaps.answer: 10 m/s directed away from the wall (taking that as positive, 4 − (−6)).

gaps.name: Examples of scalars and vectors
gaps.what: Be ready to give examples: scalars include mass, time, energy, power, charge, density, speed; vectors include force, weight, momentum, impulse, displacement, velocity, acceleration.
gaps.check: Is each a scalar or vector: work done, momentum, current, weight?
gaps.answer: Work: scalar; momentum: vector; current: scalar at AS; weight: vector.

gaps.name: Small-angle approximation
gaps.what: For small angles in radians, sin θ ≈ tan θ ≈ θ and cos θ ≈ 1; this is why fringe spacing gives λ = ax/D.
gaps.check: Why is λ = ax/D only valid when a is much smaller than D?
gaps.answer: The derivation uses sin θ ≈ tan θ for small angles, true only when fringe angles are small.

gaps.name: Algebra symbols
gaps.what: Know =, <, <<, >>, >, ∝, ≈ and Δ: e.g. ≪ means much less than, ∝ proportional to, Δ a change in.
gaps.check: What does F ∝ Δp/Δt tell you?
gaps.answer: Force is proportional to the rate of change of momentum.

gaps.name: Solving quadratics
gaps.what: Equations like s = ut + ½at² can need the quadratic formula to find t; pick the physically sensible root.
gaps.check: A stone is thrown up at 10 m/s from a 15 m cliff. How long until it hits the sea?
gaps.answer: −15 = 10t − 4.905t²: t ≈ 3.2 s (reject the negative root).

gaps.name: Sketching standard relationships
gaps.what: Sketch y = kx, y = kx², y = k/x, y = k/x², y = sin x and y = cos x, including where they cross axes and asymptotes.
gaps.check: Sketch elastic potential energy against extension for a spring obeying Hooke's law.
gaps.answer: A parabola from the origin, curving upward (E = ½kx²).

gaps.name: Spreadsheet and iterative modelling
gaps.what: Rates of change can be modelled in small time steps (e.g. new v = old v + aΔt, with a recalculated each step for drag) without calculus.
gaps.check: In a step-by-step model of a falling object with drag, why does acceleration change each step?
gaps.answer: Drag depends on speed; speed changes each step, so resultant force and acceleration are recalculated.

gaps.name: Simple probability and electron waves
gaps.what: In electron diffraction, bright rings are where electrons are most likely to arrive; wave intensity relates to the probability of finding an electron there.
gaps.check: What do bright rings on an electron diffraction screen represent?
gaps.answer: Places where many electrons arrive, i.e. high probability of detection (constructive interference of electron waves).

gaps.name: Simultaneous equations
gaps.what: Two unknowns from two equations, e.g. E and r from two sets of (V, I) values using E = V + Ir.
gaps.check: A cell gives 1.40 V at 0.20 A and 1.20 V at 0.60 A. Find r and E.

gaps.name: Testing ratios in data
gaps.what: Without a graph, check proportionality by showing y/x is constant across readings (or xy constant for inverse proportion), allowing for uncertainty.
gaps.check: x = 2, 4, 6 gives y = 5.0, 10.1, 14.9. Are they proportional?
gaps.answer: y/x ≈ 2.50, 2.53, 2.48: roughly constant, so yes within uncertainty.

gaps.name: Average vs instantaneous speed
gaps.what: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time; instantaneous speed is the gradient of the tangent at one moment. They differ whenever speed changes.
gaps.check: How do you find instantaneous velocity at 3 s from a curved s–t graph?
gaps.answer: Draw a tangent at t = 3 s and calculate its gradient.

gaps.name: Acceleration–time graphs
gaps.what: The area under an acceleration–time graph is the change in velocity; a horizontal line means constant acceleration.
gaps.check: An a–t graph shows 3 m s^-2 for 4 s. What is the velocity change?
gaps.answer: Area = 3 × 4 = 12 m/s.

gaps.name: Graphs for a bouncing ball
gaps.what: On a v–t graph for a dropped bouncing ball, velocity changes sign at each bounce; gradient stays g between bounces; areas above and below the axis give displacements in opposite directions.
gaps.check: What is the gradient of the v–t graph for a bouncing ball while it is in the air?
gaps.answer: Constant, equal to g (about 9.81 m s^-2) downward, both rising and falling.

gaps.name: Projectile at the highest point
gaps.what: For a projectile launched at an angle, vertical velocity is zero at the top but horizontal velocity is unchanged, so the speed there is the horizontal component, not zero.
gaps.check: A ball is kicked at 20 m/s at 30 degrees. What is its speed at the top?
gaps.answer: 20 cos 30° ≈ 17 m/s (only horizontal velocity remains).

gaps.name: Air resistance on a projectile
gaps.what: With air resistance, a projectile reaches a lower height and shorter range, and its path is no longer symmetrical (steeper descent).
gaps.check: How does air resistance change the shape of a projectile's path?
gaps.answer: Lower maximum height, shorter range, and a steeper, asymmetric descent.

gaps.name: Weight components on a slope
gaps.what: On an incline at angle θ, weight resolves into mg sin θ down the slope and mg cos θ into the slope (balanced by normal contact force).
gaps.check: A 2.0 kg block rests on a frictionless 30 degree slope. What is its acceleration?
gaps.answer: a = g sin 30° ≈ 4.9 m s^-2 down the slope.

gaps.name: Lifts and apparent weight
gaps.what: In a lift, the normal force (scale reading) = m(g + a) when accelerating upward and m(g − a) when accelerating downward; it equals mg at constant velocity.
gaps.check: A 60 kg person is in a lift accelerating upward at 2 m s^-2. What does a scale read?

gaps.name: Connected bodies and pulleys
gaps.what: For objects joined by a string, treat the system as one mass for acceleration, then use one body's free-body diagram to find tension.
gaps.check: A 2 kg trolley on a frictionless table is pulled by a 1 kg hanging mass. Find the acceleration.

gaps.name: Drag proportional to v squared
gaps.what: At everyday speeds in air, drag is roughly proportional to speed squared, so doubling speed quadruples drag (and greatly increases power needed: P = Dv).
gaps.check: If drag ∝ v², how does the power needed against drag change when speed doubles?
gaps.answer: Drag × 4 and speed × 2, so power × 8.

gaps.name: Parachute and skydiver motion
gaps.what: Opening a parachute raises drag above weight so the diver decelerates until a new, lower terminal velocity is reached; acceleration is upward during that phase.
gaps.check: Sketch and explain v–t after a parachute opens.
gaps.answer: Velocity falls steeply then levels off at a lower terminal velocity as drag decreases back to equal weight.

gaps.name: Toppling and stability
gaps.what: An object topples when the line of action of its weight passes outside its base; a low centre of gravity and wide base increase stability.
gaps.check: Why does a tall cupboard topple more easily than a low, wide one?
gaps.answer: Its weight's line of action moves outside its base at a smaller tilt angle.

gaps.name: Weight of a uniform object acts at its centre
gaps.what: For a uniform beam or rod the weight acts at its midpoint; use this distance in moments calculations.
gaps.check: A uniform 3 m plank of weight 200 N is pivoted at one end. What is the moment of its weight?

gaps.name: Closed triangle of forces
gaps.what: Three coplanar forces in equilibrium form a closed triangle when drawn head to tail; use it (or resolving) to find an unknown force.
gaps.check: A picture hangs from two strings. How can a triangle of forces find the tensions?
gaps.answer: Draw weight and the two tension directions head to tail to close a triangle; side lengths give the tensions.

gaps.name: Atmospheric pressure and pressure at depth
gaps.what: Air pressure at sea level is about 100 kPa. hρg gives the extra pressure from a fluid column, independent of container shape; total pressure = atmospheric + hρg.
gaps.check: What is the total pressure 10 m under water?

gaps.name: Upthrust from a pressure difference
gaps.what: Pressure is greater on the bottom of an immersed object than the top, so there is a net upward force; this upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced.
gaps.check: Explain why a submerged block experiences upthrust.
gaps.answer: Pressure increases with depth, so the upward force on the lower face exceeds the downward force on the top face.

gaps.name: Floating objects
gaps.what: A floating object displaces its own weight of fluid; fraction submerged = object density ÷ fluid density.
gaps.check: A wooden block of density 600 kg m^-3 floats in water. What fraction is submerged?

gaps.name: Derive Ek = ½mv²
gaps.what: From rest, a constant force F over distance s does work Fs = mas, and v² = 2as, so Fs = ½mv².
gaps.check: Derive the kinetic energy formula from work done and suvat.
gaps.answer: W = Fs = (ma)s; v² = 2as so as = v²/2; W = ½mv².

gaps.name: Derive Ep = mgh
gaps.what: Lifting at constant speed needs force equal to weight mg; work done over height h is mgh, stored as gravitational potential energy.
gaps.check: Derive the gravitational potential energy equation.
gaps.answer: Force = weight = mg; work = force × distance = mgh, which becomes GPE.

gaps.name: Derive P = Fv
gaps.what: Power = work/time = Fx/t, and x/t = v at constant speed, so P = Fv.
gaps.check: Show that power equals force times velocity.
gaps.answer: P = W/t = Fx/t = F(x/t) = Fv.

gaps.name: Work against resistive forces
gaps.what: Work done against friction or drag is transferred to thermal energy of the surroundings; it explains why final KE is less than lost GPE.
gaps.check: A cyclist freewheels downhill, losing 4000 J of GPE but gaining 3000 J KE. Where did the rest go?
gaps.answer: 1000 J did work against friction and air resistance, heating the surroundings.

gaps.name: Braking distance proportional to v squared
gaps.what: With a constant braking force, F × braking distance = ½mv², so braking distance ∝ v²; thinking distance ∝ v (fixed reaction time).
gaps.check: A car's speed doubles. What happens to thinking and braking distances?
gaps.answer: Thinking distance doubles; braking distance quadruples.

gaps.name: Speed checks and cameras
gaps.what: Average-speed cameras time a car between two points a known distance apart; spot cameras use two images a known time apart and road markings.
gaps.check: How do average-speed cameras calculate speed?
gaps.answer: Distance between cameras divided by the time between the two recorded number-plate images.

gaps.name: Elastic limit vs limit of proportionality
gaps.what: Limit of proportionality: end of the straight part. Elastic limit: beyond it the material does not return to its original length. They are close but not the same point.
gaps.check: A wire is loaded just past its elastic limit then unloaded. What do you observe?
gaps.answer: It is permanently extended (plastic deformation); it doesn't return to its original length.

gaps.name: ½Fx needs Hooke's law
gaps.what: E = ½Fx and ½kx² only apply to the linear (Hooke's law) region; beyond it, find the area under the curve by counting squares.
gaps.check: When can you not use E = ½kx² for a stretched band?
gaps.answer: When force is not proportional to extension (beyond the limit of proportionality or for rubber).

gaps.name: Young modulus is a material property
gaps.what: Young modulus depends only on the material, not its dimensions; the force constant k depends on length and area (k = EA/L).
gaps.check: Two wires of the same steel, one twice as long. Compare their Young modulus and force constant.
gaps.answer: Same Young modulus; the longer wire has half the force constant.

gaps.name: Examples of material types
gaps.what: Ductile: copper, steel (drawn into wires, large plastic region). Brittle: glass, cast iron, ceramics (fracture with little plastic deformation). Polymeric: rubber, polythene.
gaps.check: Give one example each of ductile, brittle and polymeric materials.
gaps.answer: Copper; glass; rubber.

gaps.name: Car safety features
gaps.what: Crumple zones, airbags and seat belts increase the time over which momentum changes, reducing the force; mandatory seat belts show science informing law.
gaps.check: Use F = Δp/Δt to explain how an airbag reduces injury.
gaps.answer: Same change in momentum over a longer time gives a smaller average force on the person.

gaps.name: Rebound momentum change
gaps.what: When an object reverses direction, Δp = m(v + u) using speeds, because the signs differ; the force on a wall is larger than for an object that stops.
gaps.check: A 0.20 kg ball hits a wall at 5 m/s and rebounds at 3 m/s. Find Δp.
gaps.answer: 0.20 × (3 + 5) = 1.6 kg m/s away from the wall.

gaps.name: Force from a stream of mass
gaps.what: For a jet of water, air or sand, force = (mass per second) × change in velocity; mass per second = ρ × A × v.
gaps.check: Water hits a wall at 4 m/s at 2 kg per second and stops. What force acts?

gaps.name: Relative speed in elastic collisions
gaps.what: Kinetic energy is conserved only in perfectly elastic collisions; then the speed of approach equals the speed of separation. Total energy is always conserved.
gaps.check: How can you show a collision is inelastic from data?
gaps.answer: Calculate total kinetic energy before and after; if it has decreased, the collision is inelastic.

gaps.name: Charges of electron and proton
gaps.what: An electron has charge −e and a proton +e (e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C); an ion's charge is a whole-number multiple of e.
gaps.check: What is the charge on an ion that has lost two electrons?

gaps.name: Conductors, semiconductors, insulators by n
gaps.what: Metals have very large n (about 10^28–10^29 m^-3), semiconductors much smaller and rising with temperature, insulators very small; for the same current, smaller n means larger drift velocity.
gaps.check: Why is the drift velocity higher in a semiconductor than a metal for the same current and area?
gaps.answer: I = Anev: semiconductors have far smaller n, so v must be larger.

gaps.name: Drift speed is slow
gaps.what: Drift velocities in metals are typically under a millimetre per second, yet a lamp lights instantly because electrons all along the circuit start moving together.
gaps.check: If drift speed is so slow, why does a lamp light almost instantly?
gaps.answer: Free electrons are throughout the wire; the electric field reaches them all almost at once, so they all start drifting.

gaps.name: Drift velocity in thinner wire
gaps.what: In series sections of the same metal, current is the same, so drift velocity is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area (v ∝ 1/A, so v ∝ 1/d²).
gaps.check: Wire B has half the diameter of wire A in series. Compare drift velocities.
gaps.answer: Area is a quarter, so drift velocity in B is 4 times that in A.

gaps.name: Number density from atomic data
gaps.what: If each atom gives one free electron, n = (density × Avogadro constant) ÷ molar mass, using N_A from the data sheet.
gaps.check: Copper has density 8900 kg m^-3 and molar mass 0.0635 kg/mol. Estimate n.

gaps.name: Thermistor I–V characteristic
gaps.what: For an NTC thermistor the I–V graph curves upward (away from the V axis): as current heats it, resistance falls, so current rises faster than p.d.
gaps.check: Sketch and explain the I–V graph for an NTC thermistor.
gaps.answer: Curve gets steeper with p.d.; heating lowers resistance as more charge carriers are released.

gaps.name: Diode and LED threshold p.d.
gaps.what: A diode conducts only above a threshold p.d. in forward bias (about 0.6 V for silicon; around 1.5–3 V for LEDs, depending on colour); in reverse bias its resistance is very high.
gaps.check: Why is a diode's resistance very large below about 0.6 V?
gaps.answer: Almost no current flows until the threshold p.d. is reached, so R = V/I is very large.

gaps.name: Why a filament lamp's resistance rises
gaps.what: Higher current heats the filament; metal ions vibrate more, so electrons collide more often, reducing drift and raising resistance.
gaps.check: Explain in terms of particles why lamp resistance increases with current.
gaps.answer: Higher temperature makes lattice ions vibrate more, so electrons collide more frequently, increasing resistance.

gaps.name: Resistivity change: metals vs semiconductors
gaps.what: Metals: n stays constant; resistivity rises slightly with temperature from more ion vibrations. Semiconductors (thermistors, LDRs): heat or light frees many more carriers, so resistance falls.
gaps.check: Why does an LDR's resistance fall when light intensity rises?
gaps.answer: More charge carriers are freed, so number density n increases and resistance decreases.

gaps.name: Potentiometer as a potential divider
gaps.what: A potentiometer (a resistor with a sliding contact connected as a divider) can provide any output p.d. from zero to the supply p.d., unlike a series variable resistor.
gaps.check: Why use a potentiometer rather than a variable resistor in series to vary a lamp's p.d. down to zero?
gaps.answer: A potentiometer output can go to 0 V; a series resistor can only reduce the p.d., never to zero.

gaps.name: Designing a sensing circuit
gaps.what: In a divider, the output across a component rises when its share of resistance rises; place the LDR or thermistor so V out rises (or falls) as required.
gaps.check: A thermistor is in series with a fixed resistor. Across which should V out be taken so it rises with temperature?
gaps.answer: Across the fixed resistor: the thermistor's resistance falls, so the fixed resistor's share of p.d. rises.

gaps.name: Ideal meters and voltmeter loading
gaps.what: An ideal ammeter has zero resistance and an ideal voltmeter infinite resistance; a real voltmeter in parallel with a large resistor lowers the combined resistance and changes readings.
gaps.check: Why must a voltmeter have very high resistance?
gaps.answer: So it draws negligible current and does not change the p.d. it measures.

gaps.name: E.m.f.s in series and opposition
gaps.what: Cells in series aiding add their e.m.f.s and internal resistances; cells facing opposite ways subtract. Identical cells in parallel keep the same e.m.f. with lower internal resistance.
gaps.check: Two 1.5 V cells are connected in series but one is reversed. What is the net e.m.f.?
gaps.answer: Zero: the e.m.f.s cancel.

gaps.name: Choosing internal resistance for a use
gaps.what: A car battery needs very low internal resistance to deliver a huge starting current; high-voltage supplies have high internal resistance to limit current for safety. Energy wasted in r is I²r.
gaps.check: Why do EHT supplies have a large internal resistance?
gaps.answer: It limits the current if shorted or touched, making them safer.

gaps.name: Short-circuit current
gaps.what: With zero external resistance, the maximum current is E/r and all energy is dissipated inside the source, which can overheat.
gaps.check: A 9.0 V battery with r = 2.0 Ω is short-circuited. What current flows?

gaps.name: Maximum power to a load
gaps.what: Power delivered to an external resistor is greatest when its resistance equals the source's internal resistance; beyond AS core but sometimes set as data analysis.
gaps.check: For a cell with r = 1.5 Ω, which load resistance receives most power?
gaps.answer: 1.5 Ω (equal to the internal resistance).

gaps.name: Cost of electrical energy
gaps.what: Cost = energy in kW h × price per kW h; energy (kW h) = power (kW) × time (h). Link with efficiency to compare devices.
gaps.check: A 2.5 kW heater runs 3 hours at 30p per kW h. Cost?

gaps.name: Energy-saving lamps
gaps.what: LED lamps give the same light output for far less power than filament lamps, saving energy and money and reducing emissions from power stations.
gaps.check: A 60 W filament bulb is replaced by a 10 W LED. Energy saved in 1000 h?

gaps.name: Reading displacement–distance and displacement–time graphs
gaps.what: A displacement–distance graph is a snapshot (wavelength from repeat length); a displacement–time graph is one point over time (period from repeat). Longitudinal waves are shown the same way, with compressions and rarefactions.
gaps.check: From which wave graph can you read the period directly?
gaps.answer: A displacement–time graph for one point on the wave.

gaps.name: Frequency unchanged on refraction
gaps.what: When a wave enters a new medium its speed and wavelength change but its frequency stays the same (set by the source); slowing down bends it toward the normal.
gaps.check: Light enters glass (n = 1.5) from air. What happens to its speed, frequency and wavelength?
gaps.answer: Speed and wavelength fall by a factor 1.5; frequency stays the same.

gaps.name: When diffraction is significant
gaps.what: Diffraction is most noticeable when the gap or obstacle is about the same size as the wavelength, e.g. sound spreading through doorways, long radio waves bending round hills.
gaps.check: Why can you hear but not see someone around a doorway?
gaps.answer: Sound wavelengths (~1 m) are similar to the doorway width; light's (~500 nm) are far smaller, so light hardly diffracts.

gaps.name: Intensity from a point source
gaps.what: Power spreads over a sphere of area 4πr² (data sheet), so I = P/(4πr²): doubling distance quarters the intensity.
gaps.check: A 0.60 W source radiates equally. What is the intensity 2.0 m away?

gaps.name: Nature of EM waves
gaps.what: EM waves are transverse oscillations of electric and magnetic fields at right angles; they need no medium, travel at c in a vacuum, and can all be polarised, reflected, refracted and diffracted.
gaps.check: State two properties shared by all electromagnetic waves.
gaps.answer: Transverse; travel at 3.00 × 10^8 m/s in a vacuum (also: can be polarised, need no medium).

gaps.name: Polarisation applications
gaps.what: Polaroid sunglasses cut glare because reflected light is partly polarised; TV/radio aerials must align with the transmitted polarisation; LCD screens use polarisers.
gaps.check: Why do Polaroid sunglasses reduce glare from water?
gaps.answer: Light reflected off water is partly plane polarised; the filter is aligned to absorb that orientation.

gaps.name: Refractive index of air and n ≥ 1
gaps.what: Refractive index of air is taken as 1.00 (vacuum exactly 1); every material has n of 1 or more because light is never faster than c.
gaps.check: Why can't a material have refractive index 0.8?
gaps.answer: It would mean light travels faster than c in it (v = c/n), which is impossible.

gaps.name: Optical fibres
gaps.what: Optical fibres keep light in by total internal reflection; cladding of lower refractive index protects the core and prevents signal leakage. Used in endoscopes and communications.
gaps.check: Why must the cladding have a lower refractive index than the core?
gaps.answer: TIR only occurs going from higher to lower refractive index, so light stays in the core.

gaps.name: Adding waves graphically
gaps.what: To show superposition, add the displacements of two waves point by point at each position or time to sketch the resultant.
gaps.check: Two waves meet with displacements +3 mm and −1 mm at a point. What is the resultant?
gaps.answer: +2 mm.

gaps.name: Producing coherent sources
gaps.what: Two separate lamps are not coherent; use a laser (or one source through two slits). Two loudspeakers or microwave slits fed from one source are coherent.
gaps.check: Why can't two separate light bulbs produce a visible interference pattern?
gaps.answer: Their phase relationship changes randomly, so they are not coherent and fringes don't stay still.

gaps.name: Young's experiment as evidence
gaps.what: Young's double-slit fringes gave classical evidence that light is a wave, supporting Huygens over Newton's particle (corpuscular) idea; later the photoelectric effect revived a particle model.
gaps.check: What did Young's double-slit experiment show about light?
gaps.answer: Light interferes, so it behaves as a wave.

gaps.name: Changing a double-slit pattern
gaps.what: Fringe spacing x = λD/a: wider for longer λ (red), larger D, or narrower slit separation. White light gives a white central fringe with coloured fringes either side.
gaps.check: What pattern is seen with white light through a double slit?
gaps.answer: Central white fringe, then coloured fringes (blue nearest centre, red outermost) fading out.

gaps.name: Stationary vs progressive waves compared
gaps.what: Stationary: no net energy transfer, amplitude varies with position (zero at nodes), points between adjacent nodes in phase. Progressive: energy transferred, same amplitude everywhere, phase varies continuously.
gaps.check: Give two differences between stationary and progressive waves.
gaps.answer: Stationary waves don't transfer energy; amplitude varies with position (nodes and antinodes) unlike progressive waves.

gaps.name: Phase in a stationary wave
gaps.what: All points between two adjacent nodes move in phase; points in neighbouring loops are in antiphase (180 degrees).
gaps.check: What is the phase difference between points on either side of a node?
gaps.answer: 180 degrees (π rad).

gaps.name: Why the wave model fails
gaps.what: Wave theory predicts any frequency would eject electrons given enough intensity or time; observed threshold frequency and instant emission need photons. Light shows wave (interference) and particle (photoelectric) behaviour.
gaps.check: Why does the photoelectric effect support the photon model?
gaps.answer: Emission depends on frequency not intensity and is instant: each electron absorbs one photon's energy hf.

gaps.name: KEmax against frequency graph
gaps.what: Plotting KEmax against f gives a straight line: gradient = h, f-intercept = threshold frequency, extrapolated y-intercept = −φ. Every metal gives a parallel line.
gaps.check: What is the gradient of KEmax against frequency, and why do different metals give parallel lines?
gaps.answer: Gradient h (the same constant for all metals); only the work function, and so the intercept, differs.

gaps.name: Momentum from kinetic energy
gaps.what: p = √(2mE_k), from E_k = p²/2m; for an electron accelerated through V, λ = h/√(2meV).
gaps.check: Find λ for an electron accelerated through 150 V.

gaps.name: de Broglie wavelength of other objects
gaps.what: All particles (protons, neutrons, atoms) have λ = h/p; at the same speed heavier particles have shorter λ; everyday objects have wavelengths far too small to diffract.
gaps.check: Why does a moving cricket ball not show diffraction?
gaps.answer: Its momentum is huge, so λ = h/p is ~10^-34 m, far smaller than any gap.

gaps.name: Typical photon energies
gaps.what: Visible photons carry roughly 1.6–3.1 eV (red to violet); metal work functions are a few eV, so many metals need UV.
gaps.check: Is a 500 nm photon able to free electrons from zinc (φ = 4.3 eV)?
gaps.answer: E = hc/λ ≈ 2.5 eV < 4.3 eV, so no.

gaps.name: History of quantum ideas
gaps.what: Scientific knowledge changes: classical wave theory of light was revised by Planck's quanta and Einstein's photon explanation of the photoelectric effect, accepted after experimental confirmation and peer review.
gaps.check: Why was Einstein's photon idea eventually accepted?
gaps.answer: It explained observations the wave model could not, and experiments (e.g. Millikan's) confirmed its predictions.

gaps.name: Benefits, risks and decisions
gaps.what: Be able to weigh benefits against risks of an application (e.g. airbags, power stations, laser use) and explain how evidence informs society's decisions such as laws and consumer choice.
gaps.check: Give one benefit and one risk of airbags.
gaps.answer: Benefit: reduces force on occupants in a crash. Risk: can injure children or if deployed unexpectedly.

gaps.name: Energy stores and pathways
gaps.what: Stores: kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, chemical, nuclear, electrostatic, magnetic. Transfers happen mechanically (forces), electrically, by heating or by radiation.
gaps.check: Describe the energy changes as a battery-powered motor lifts a load.
gaps.answer: Chemical store → electrical work → gravitational store of load, with some thermal energy dissipated.

gaps.name: Particle model and density
gaps.what: Solids and liquids have closely packed particles so similar, high densities; gases are far less dense and compressible. Measure irregular object volume by displacement (eureka can).
gaps.check: How do you find the density of an irregular stone?
gaps.answer: Measure mass on a balance; find volume from water displaced in a measuring cylinder or eureka can; ρ = m/V.

gaps.name: Density of water and air
gaps.what: Water's density is about 1000 kg m^-3 (1 g cm^-3) and air's about 1.2 kg m^-3; these are often needed for upthrust and pressure but not always given.
gaps.check: What is the mass of 1 litre of water?

gaps.name: Atomic structure and free electrons
gaps.what: Atoms have a nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons around it; ions form by losing or gaining electrons. In metals some electrons are free (delocalised) and carry current.
gaps.check: Why are metals good electrical conductors?
gaps.answer: They contain many free (delocalised) electrons that can drift through the lattice.

gaps.name: Charging by friction and electron transfer
gaps.what: Objects become charged when electrons are transferred: gaining electrons makes them negative, losing electrons makes them positive. Protons do not move.
gaps.check: A polythene rod becomes negatively charged when rubbed. What has happened?
gaps.answer: Electrons have transferred onto the rod from the cloth.

gaps.name: Mains supply facts
gaps.what: UK mains is about 230 V a.c. at 50 Hz; household appliances are rated in W or kW.
gaps.check: What is the current in a 2.3 kW kettle on UK mains?

gaps.name: Sound basics
gaps.what: Sound is longitudinal, needs a medium, travels about 340 m/s in air (faster in solids); human hearing about 20 Hz–20 kHz; ultrasound is above that.
gaps.check: Can sound travel through a vacuum? Why?
gaps.answer: No: it is a mechanical (longitudinal) wave needing particles to vibrate.

gaps.name: Echoes and sonar
gaps.what: For an echo, the wave travels there and back, so distance = speed × time ÷ 2.
gaps.check: An echo returns 0.40 s after a clap at a cliff. How far is the cliff?

gaps.name: Visible spectrum order
gaps.what: Visible light runs from red (about 700 nm, lowest frequency and photon energy) to violet (about 400 nm, highest).
gaps.check: Which LED colour emits photons of greatest energy: red, green or blue?
gaps.answer: Blue, since it has the shortest wavelength.

gaps.name: Uses and hazards of EM waves
gaps.what: Radio: communication; microwaves: cooking, satellites; IR: heating, remote controls; visible: fibres, sight; UV: sterilising, causes skin damage; X-ray and gamma: imaging and treatment, ionising and harmful.
gaps.check: Which regions of the EM spectrum are ionising?
gaps.answer: High-frequency UV, X-rays and gamma rays.

gaps.name: All objects fall with the same g
gaps.what: Mass (kg) is the amount of matter; weight (N) is the gravitational force mg. Without drag, every object falls with the same acceleration g ≈ 9.81 m s^-2, whatever its mass.
gaps.check: Do a heavy and a light ball dropped together (no air resistance) land together?
gaps.answer: Yes: both accelerate at g regardless of mass.

gaps.name: Specific heat capacity
gaps.what: Energy to heat a mass m through Δθ is mcΔθ; AS questions on kettles or efficiency sometimes give c and expect this.
gaps.check: How much energy heats 0.50 kg of water by 20 K (c = 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1)?

gaps.name: Kelvin and Celsius
gaps.what: Temperature in kelvin = temperature in °C + 273; the kelvin is the SI base unit, and a change of 1 K equals a change of 1 °C.
gaps.check: Convert 27 °C to kelvin.

gaps.name: Gears, levers and pivots
gaps.what: Levers multiply force: a small force far from the pivot balances a large force near it; spanners, wheelbarrows and seesaws apply the principle of moments.
gaps.check: Why is a nut easier to undo with a longer spanner?
gaps.answer: The same force at a larger perpendicular distance gives a bigger moment.
